question: Around 900 000 parcels and packages are imported into the Union from non-EU countries each day. Most contain items that do not comply with statutory requirements. This puts consumers at risk due to numerous safety deficiencies. It is difficult to put a number on the scale of the issue, but to give an idea, the EU toys industry found deficiencies in 18 out of 19 toys tested. EU product safety regulations are not being complied with. 1.
What does the Commission intend to do to protect consumers in EU Member States, in particular children, from dangerous products from non-EU countries?

What is the Commission’s estimate of the damage that has so far been caused by the fact that manufacturers from non-EU countries are manufacturing products to completely different standards and that EU manufacturers are being severely disadvantaged?
How does the Commission intend to correct this distortion of competition and ensure sufficient and adequate market surveillance in the future?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (5.7.2024) The Commission has taken several initiatives to prevent the import of dangerous non-Union goods, including: - the Market Surveillance Regulation (EU) 2019/10201, strengthening the powers and tools of the market surveillance authorities to act against non-compliant/dangerous products, also those sold online.
It also provides a framework for increased cooperation with customs; - the Digital Services Act (EU) 2022/20652 obliging online marketplaces to identify their business users and the sellers.

They should provide users with means to flag illegal content, cooperate with ‘trusted flaggers’ for identifying and removing such content; - the General Product Safety Regulation (EU) 2023/9883 for non-food consumer products including obligations for online marketplaces and strengthening the rules to ensure that products sold in the EU are safe.

The principle is that products placed on the market in the EU must be safe and comply with the requirements laid down in EU/national legislation. Risk-based customs controls and market surveillance activities target products and economic operators which are most likely to circumvent the rules.

In 2023, the Commission proposed in the Customs Reform to increase the responsibility of ecommerce operators for the fiscal and product safety requirements applicable to the products sold to EU consumers. The proposal also includes a series of tools to enable a consistent EUapproach to proactively identifying risks in e-commerce.

In addition, the Commission proposes to remove the duty exemption that provides a competitive advantage to third country sellers of goods valued up to EUR 150. The Commission stands ready to use the available instruments, to accelerate the EU customs reform and to coordinate and strengthen the enforcement activities of public authorities.
